standard.title: Interpretations of Asia-Pacific
standard.description: interpretations about the Asian-Pacific society and events, and/or individuals and/or groups connected to the society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how historians construct and evaluate interpretations (AC9HH8K06, AC9HH8K11). They understand the events, individuals and society of the chosen Asia-Pacific context (AC9HH8K12–K15). They have not yet applied interpretive analysis to Asia-Pacific historiography — including the specific challenges posed by limited written sources, oral traditions, and post-colonial perspectives on Pacific history.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how and why historians have developed different interpretations of the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including the challenges posed by source availability, the role of oral traditions and archaeology, and how interpretations have changed as new evidence emerges.

nodes.label: Source challenges in Asia-Pacific history
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the challenges posed by the available sources for the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including gaps in the written record, the role of oral traditions, and how archaeological evidence both enables and limits historical interpretation.
nodes.minimum_width: An explanation of at least one source challenge specific to the chosen Asia-Pacific context and how it shapes historical understanding.
nodes.typical_width: Source challenges across different evidence types. Examples: the absence of a written record for Polynesian history and the resulting dependence on oral traditions, archaeology and environmental science; the challenges posed by interpreting Lapita pottery from Vanuatu as evidence of Polynesian expansion; the limitations of Chinese diplomatic accounts (Zhou Daguan) as the primary written source for Khmer daily life; how changes in interpretations of Lapita culture demonstrate the fragility of interpretations built on limited sources.
wider: For Polynesia: examine the challenges posed by the lack of written sources in understanding Polynesian history — using changes in interpretations of Lapita culture in Vanuatu as a concrete example of how new archaeological evidence can overturn established interpretations

For the Khmer: compare the stone carvings of Angkor with Zhou Daguan's written account as two different source types that produce different — and sometimes contradictory — pictures of Khmer daily life
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand the specific source challenges of Asia-Pacific history cannot critically evaluate the interpretations they encounter. The source-limitation context is prerequisite to all interpretive analysis in this standard.

response_modes.reason: Students need to understand that source limitations are not just gaps — they actively shape what kinds of interpretations are possible. Scaffold the logic: when written sources are absent, what can archaeology, oral tradition and environmental science tell us, and what remains uncertain?

success_criteria: Identifies at least one source challenge specific to the chosen Asia-Pacific context
Explains how that challenge shapes or limits the interpretations historians can make

nodes.label: Competing interpretations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe competing historical interpretations of the chosen Asia-Pacific society and explain why they differ — including how evidence, perspective and changing scholarly understanding have produced different accounts.
nodes.minimum_width: Two different interpretations of the chosen society or event with at least one explanation of why they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Competing interpretations across chosen contexts. Examples: multiple theories about the decline of the Khmer Empire — Tai invasions, Jayavarman VII's building program, population growth, religious revolution, environmental challenges, soil sterilisation, water management failure; different theories about Polynesian expansion (west-east vs east-west; accidental vs intentional); the significance of Perry's visit to Japan and competing interpretations of Tokugawa isolation.
wider: For the Khmer: discuss the multiple theories for the empire's decline — examining how each is supported by different types of evidence (political, religious, environmental, archaeological) and why no single explanation is universally accepted

For Polynesia: evaluate the significance of competing theories about Polynesian expansion — considering what is at stake in the debate between accidental and intentional navigation for how we understand Pacific peoples' agency and capability

response_modes.reason: The range of interpretive contests in Asia-Pacific history — from Khmer decline to Polynesian expansion to Japanese isolation — is wide. Using more than one context prevents students from treating interpretive diversity as specific to one case.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The debate between accidental and intentional Polynesian expansion is unusually rich — it is not just a historical question but one that bears on how Pacific peoples' capabilities and agency are understood. This connects historiography to contemporary identity and cultural politics in ways that deepen students' appreciation of why interpretations matter.
success_criteria: Describes at least two competing interpretations of the chosen Asia-Pacific society or event
Explains at least one reason why the interpretations differ, with reference to evidence, perspective or changing scholarship

nodes.label: Evaluating interpretations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate competing interpretations of the chosen Asia-Pacific society — identifying which is better supported by evidence and explaining what the interpretive debate reveals about the nature of historical knowledge.
nodes.minimum_width: An evaluation of at least one interpretation using evidence to assess its strengths or limitations.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluation of competing interpretations using source evidence; the significance of Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate and the impact of Perry's visit; the Polynesian expansion debate evaluated against archaeological and environmental evidence; the Khmer decline theories assessed for evidential support.
wider: For Japan: evaluate the significance of the range of reasons for Japan's closure to foreigners under the Tokugawa Shogunate and assess the impact of Perry's visit (1853) — examining both the interpretation that isolation was a strength and the interpretation that it created vulnerability

For Polynesia: evaluate how each expansion theory (accidental vs intentional; west-east vs east-west) is supported by different types of evidence, and consider what accepting one interpretation over another means for our understanding of Pacific peoples

response_modes.reason: Evaluation integrates source-challenge analysis (Node 1) and competing-interpretation identification (Node 2). Invest in helping students move from noting that interpretations differ to making a reasoned judgement about which is better supported and why.

success_criteria: Evaluates at least one interpretation of the chosen Asia-Pacific society using evidence
Explains what the interpretive debate reveals about the nature of historical knowledge — including the role of evidence, perspective and the limits of sources
